doc.title: Junior Mance Part I interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, New York City, New York, July 27, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Playing Stan Kenton's charts before Kenton's band
summary: The band opens for Kenton and plays his charts; his musicians sit in at rehearsal.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: Harold was a frustrated trumpet player himself. But he was a good musician, he knew about the theory of music. So he would trade bands a set of uniforms if they let him copy like some of the tunes from their book. Like we had tunes from Basie’s book, and remember the Billy Eckstine Big Band? We had some of those tunes. We had a couple of Dizzy’s tunes. We had a lot of Stan Kenton tunes, some Woody Herman things. The book was about that thick with all these things, you know all these charts. And we got all these great players, especially with Gene and Lee. And so we’d get together every week and the band was like tight, it was just perfect. In fact I remember once Stan Kenton came to Chicago to play a dance. In those days they had more dances than concerts. And so we got the gig for the opening act for Stan. So I don’t know why Harold did this, with all of the stuff we had in the book, he played all of Stan Kenton’s charts. He called all of Stan Kenton’s charts. So while we were playing, you know like the cats are coming to work out of Stan’s band, and here we were playing. So I looked up once and they’re lined up behind our bandstand listening. And one of them yelled out “see man, that’s the way that’s supposed to sound.” I said whoa. And Stan was, oh he was pissed. So the guys came on, and it was funny to the guys in Stan’s band. And we played other things too after a while, but Stan was, oh man, he was really burned, because we played his tunes. So the next night the band had a layover for a day. We had a rehearsal. And Stan’s whole band showed up at our rehearsal, just to sit in and play with us at the rehearsal. And then there were a lot of little things that they had done different in the arrangements. Like a couple of the trumpet players were working with the trumpet section, you know, there were a couple of saxophone players the same way. Stan didn’t show up so I had no help.
That’s kind of funny and kind of beautiful also, when you talk about the way that information is shared. Because all of the information is really not on the printed page.
Right. Yeah. And this is what the guys were doing when they showed up. And we had a ball. The guys loved it.
And also this is something else I’d like you to say a word about, is how the music, when it’s played well, creates its own camaraderie.

Yes. That’s true. It does. In more than one situation the same thing would happen on the 100 Gold Fingers Tour. The camaraderie that was created by the way that everybody’s just really playing, and playing good. But in the case of the band we were playing and this guy just yelled out, I don’t even know who it was, but I remember it was one of the guys in the band, he was sort of behind the stands, he says, “Yeah, see, that’s the way it’s supposed to sound.”
He could be looking for a job himself.
I don’t know if Stan was around then, but Stan got there in time to hear us playing his stuff.
